notes:
I've organised these notes by verse, with a URL after each point. The main split is over whether Isaiah 35 describes a future earthly kingdom for Israel or the gospel age and the church. I found nothing from the Lutheran sites, netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, or from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, so those are left out. The Catholic view comes from the Haydock commentary hosted on biblehub, not from newadvent.org or catholic.com. Points from the Haydock and Cambridge Bible pages are summarised without citation markers, but each has its URL.

**Chapter overview**
- Isaiah 35 follows the judgment on Edom in chapter 34. This chapter stands in stark contrast to the bleak picture of slaughter and desolation in the preceding chapter. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-35-commentary
- **This is where traditions really differ.**
  - *Dispensational (Precept Austin, which collects MacArthur, Vine and Constable):* the chapter is about physical blessings to the nation of Israel in anticipation of their deliverance by the Messiah at His Second Coming followed by establishment of His Millennial Kingdom. The return from Babylon only foreshadows it. The page says this rules out postmillennialism, and that the amillennial view (that these promises are fulfilled in the church) is foreign to Isaiah's thought. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-35-commentary
  - *Guzik (Calvary Chapel):* the promise works on three levels. It was fulfilled when Judah recovered after the Assyrian invasion, is true in the longer term as modern-day Israel has turned the wilderness and the wasteland into productive farms, and will be fully fulfilled after the tribulation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
  - *Reformed (Geneva Study Bible):* the chapter prophecies of the full restoration of the Church both of the Jews and Gentiles under Christ, which will be fully accomplished at the last day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-1.htm
  - *Pulpit Commentary:* after God's enemies are punished, the peace, prosperity, and glory of his Church will follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-1.htm
  - *Biblical Illustrator:* the promise is primarily and chiefly to the Jews, referring to their final restoration to their own land in the last days. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/isaiah-35.html

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: the three words for "desert" mean the wild pasture-land, the bare moor, the sandy steppe. The "rose" is better translated narcissus or crocus. The renewed land is a picture of the "Paradise of God" (Revelation 2:7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Barnes: the wilderness is "moral" and stands for the whole pagan world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-1.htm
- Gill (Baptist) leans toward the Gentile church in the latter day, after the destruction of antichrist. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-1.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): it is Emmanuel's land, or the seat of God's church and people, which will flourish. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html
- Precept Austin: a literal reversal of the curse of Genesis 3 at the start of the Millennium. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-35-commentary
- Guzik links the verse to Romans 8: Nature is waiting for the transformation that will come when the Messiah reigns. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
- Haydock (Catholic): Judah flourished under Hezekiah, but the Church flourishes more after Christ, and the Gentiles will be converted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon are three kinds of cultivated beauty set against the three kinds of desert in v. 1. Over the land shines not the common light of day, but the glory of Jehovah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Wesley: "the glory" means the glorious discoveries of God's power and goodness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html
- Cambridge Bible (older critical scholarship): compare "they shall see the glory of the Lord" with Isaiah 40:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/35.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: this is figurative, as its use in Hebrews 12:12 shows, and that so far suggest a like interpretation for what follows. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/35-3.htm
- Who is being told to strengthen others?
  - Wesley: Ye ministers of God, comfort and encourage God's people.
  - The Geneva Bible notes: everyone is to encourage one another, and especially the ministers to exhort and strengthen the weak.
  - Haydock: the prophets are to comfort the people, and the apostles taught the Gentiles to do good.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-3.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm
- Guzik: hands are for working and knees are for making progress and for praying, so Those with feeble knees are not progressing with the LORD and praying as they should. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/

**v. 4**
- Calvin (Reformed): the vengeance is aimed against wicked men and enemies of the Church, so it frightens them but comforts believers. https://ccel.org/study/Isaiah_35
- Ellicott: comfort rests on God's government being essentially a righteous government, punishing the oppressor, and saving the oppressed. He links the verse to Hezekiah's speech in 2 Chronicles 32:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Grammar: the Hebrew can be read as an exclamation, "God will come, vengeance! even God, a recompense!" (JFB). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-35.html
- When does God "come"?
  - Wesley: He will shortly come in the flesh, to execute vengeance upon the enemies of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html
  - Gill: Christ's first coming saves from sin. His spiritual coming, at the latter day will save his people from their antichristian enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/35-4.html
  - Constable (dispensational): God will reward the remnant, who will enter Messiah's millennial kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-35-commentary
  - Haydock: Christ will satisfy the Father's justice and bring the devil under subjection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm

**vv. 5–6a**
- **Literal or spiritual healing? Commentators disagree.**
  - Ellicott: these are spiritual infirmities, and Christ's miracles are a fulfilment ex abundante, and as a pledge and earnest of something beyond themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
  - Keil–Delitzsch (as quoted on Biblehub): The bodily defects mentioned here there is no reason for regarding as figurative representations of spiritual defects. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-6.htm
  - Pulpit: Jesus claims these words in Matthew 11:4–5. His bodily healings were also "types" of the spiritual healing he keeps doing in his Church, and Isaiah meant both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-5.htm
  - Barnes: the passage doubtless refers to the miracles which he would perform. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-5.htm
  - Cambridge (older critical scholarship): how far the language is figurative "may be difficult to say". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/35.htm
- Guzik: When God's salvation comes, miraculous power comes with it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
- Gill: fulfilled literally at Christ's first coming, spiritually through the apostles, and more fully when the blind Jews are converted. Note that this quotation isn't in the source text; Gill's words are in the fetched page: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-5.htm
- MacLaren: the "coming" includes the return from exile, Christ's first coming and his second coming. The blind, deaf, lame and mute stand for Christ restoring our ability to know, to act and to speak. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-5.htm
- Wesley: The poor Gentiles, who before were blind and deaf, shall now have the eyes and ears of their minds opened. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html
- Haydock: the Saviour healed both soul and body, as Luke 7:22 and Matthew 11:5 show. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm

**vv. 6b–7**
- The Hebrew word in v. 7 means mirage. Instead of that delusive show, there shall be in the renewed earth the lake itself. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Cambridge adds that the older reading "parched ground" fits Jewish usage, and calls the jackal clause in v. 7 text that "appears to have suffered extensive mutilation". (This wording is in the fetched page, not the cited sentence.) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/35.htm
- Wesley: the water mainly means the plentiful effusion of God's grace upon such persons and nations, as had been wholly destitute of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html
- Pulpit: The wilderness of humanity shall be renovated by a large effluence of God's grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-6.htm
- Haydock: "Baptism has sanctified the most wicked." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm
- Guzik links the streams to the Spirit in John 7:38–39 and says There is no reason for a Christian to endure a "dry time". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
- Precept Austin: a literal change to the earth's climate, landscape, plants and animals in the Messiah's age. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-35-commentary

**v. 8**
- The word for highway means a raised causeway (Ellicott, JFB). Ellicott says it is not the road home from Babylon but the road by which the pilgrims of all nations shall journey to the mountain of the Lord's house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Gill (Baptist): the highway is principally of Christ, the only way of life and salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-8.htm
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon on the greatest triumph of engineering, a way from sin to holiness, and says you are only allowed on it if you are cleansed by the great work of the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
- **What does "fools will not stray" mean? Views differ:**
  - Barnes: the way of salvation shall be so plain, that no one, however ignorant and unlearned, need err in regard to it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-8.htm
  - Guzik: there are "guardrails". God keeps even immature believers on the road. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
  - Matthew Henry: travellers won't be "guilty of any fatal misconduct", which is not the same as never making mistakes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/35-8.html
  - Constable: Fools, the morally perverse, will not wander onto it because they are unholy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/35-8.html
  - Cambridge: the Hebrew word for fool implies moral perversity, not just inexperience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/35.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): "holiness" means The people (walking in it) shall be all righteous. The road is for the weak, and blind, and lame, whom God will lead and save. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-35.html
- Pulpit and others prefer the alternative reading "he shall be with them": God walks with the travellers. Calvin notes the clause has been tortured in various ways by commentators. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-8.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/35-8.html
- **Catholic vs Protestant:** Haydock says the way is fulfilled only in the Catholic Church. The simple may learn what is necessary for salvation, but he says this will never happen "by consulting Scripture alone". This is a direct contrast with Barnes' "plain way" reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm
- Bible.org (Utley) links the highway theme to the coming of the Messiah and says it may point to "repentance" as a lifestyle. https://lists.bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-35

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: lions still roamed the Jordan valley, and the northern kingdom had recently lost much of its population, which gave the image real force. "Redeemed" means release or freedom without implying, as the English words do, a payment as its condition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Guzik: the lion is the devil of 1 Peter 5:8, and that lion has never yet devoured anyone who stayed on the road. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-35/
- Expositor's Dictionary: Satan can't harm us Because we have been redeemed out of his power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/edt/isaiah-35.html
- Haydock: the devil's power will be held back, so that no one is deceived except by their own fault. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/isaiah/35.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: a picture carrying the thoughts of men beyond any possible earthly fulfilment. It probably draws on pilgrims singing the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134), and is echoed in Revelation 7:17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/35.htm
- Benson (Methodist): the words are far too magnificent and emphatical to be answered by the mere return of the Jews. They are about the gospel age and heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-10.htm
- Gill: the ransomed "return" in the sense of being converted, and join a gospel church. Their joy is everlasting because its foundation is God's everlasting love, even though the feeling is often interrupted. The verse also applies to heaven and the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-10.htm
- Barnes: "joy upon their heads" may mean a joyful face, anointing oil or a festive garland. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/35-10.htm
- Sermon Bible: fulfilled to the individual saint when his earthly career terminates... To the saints as a body... at the times of the restitution of all things. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/isaiah-35.html
- Cambridge (older critical scholarship): the verse appears word for word in Isaiah 51:11. The chapter is full of echoes of chapters 40 and following. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/35.htm
